# Pre-Meeting DDQ Questions in Capital Introduction October 2026


A lot of managers focus their cap intro energy on the pitch. The allocator's team, meanwhile, has already been reviewing your questionnaire responses, cross-referencing them against prior submissions, and deciding whether you clear their threshold. By the time you're thinking about the meeting, they may have already made their call.


**TLDR:**


- Capital introduction arranges the meeting only; it does not prepare materials, negotiate terms, or track commitments.
- Your pre-meeting DDQ covers 7 categories including fund economics, track record, and ODD-level infrastructure questions now appearing at the intake stage.
- Allocators cross-reference your DDQ against Form ADV and prior filings; inconsistencies trigger quiet disqualifications before a human reviews your submission.
- Every DDQ question operates on two levels: the literal question on the page, and the unspoken one about whether you operate with institutional discipline.
- GovernGPT's knowledge graph surfaces responses consistent with a manager's full submission history, so allocators running cross-reference checks find nothing to flag.


## What Capital Introduction Actually Is


Capital introduction is the arranged meeting, nothing more. A prime broker, advisory firm, or conference organizer connects a fund manager with a prospective allocator. What happens after that introduction is entirely the manager's responsibility.


As[Praxis Rock puts it](https://praxisrock.com/insights/capital-introduction) , capital introduction services "stop at the meeting. They do not prepare materials, coach pitches, follow up, negotiate terms or manage diligence."


Prime brokers run the most common cap intro programs, offering introductions as part of their broader prime services relationship. Independent advisory firms and conference organizers play a similar role, particularly for newer managers without prime broker access. In each case, the arrangement is the same: a warm introduction to an allocator who has agreed to take the meeting.


What cap intro does not include: commitment tracking, term negotiation, materials preparation, or conversion accountability. The manager who mistakes an introduction for a fundraising mandate typically learns the distinction after six to twelve months of meetings that produced no capital.


## How Capital Introduction Differs from Placement Agents


Placement agents own the outcome. They build materials, manage follow-up, negotiate terms, and stay in the process until capital closes. Their compensation reflects that accountability, typically a percentage of committed capital. Cap intro introduces and exits.


The distinction matters because the two serve different needs. A placement agent is appropriate when a manager needs[AI fundraising DDQ](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/ai-fundraising-ddq-private-equity-hedge-funds) infrastructure around a raise. Cap intro is appropriate when the manager already has that infrastructure and simply needs access to a specific allocator audience.


Neither replaces the other. A manager running a formal placement engagement might still benefit from a prime broker's cap intro network for parallel introductions. The mistake is assuming that access to allocators is the same as a managed path to capital.


## When Cap Intro Works and When It Doesn't


Cap intro works when the manager has something the allocator can verify before the meeting. A verifiable track record, fund scale, and a strategy that fits within the allocator's mandate are the baseline conditions. Without them, the introduction produces a meeting that neither party will follow up on.


Prime broker programs carry a structural bias toward hedge funds. The relationships these desks maintain skew toward liquid strategies and institutional-sized tickets. A manager in private credit or real assets may find that the same network filling a hedge fund's calendar produces far fewer productive introductions.


Where cap intro works well and where it breaks down follows a recognizable pattern.


When Cap Intro Works When It Doesn't


Audited track record with verifiable performance data First-time funds without a verifiable track record


Fund scale and strategy fit within the allocator's mandate Sub-scale vehicles that don't meet institutional thresholds


Managers entering new geographies or allocator types Highly idiosyncratic or niche strategies with a small allocator pool


Liquid strategies suited to prime broker networks Private credit or real assets: prime broker networks skew toward hedge funds


Institutional back-office infrastructure already in place Managers still building their back-office foundation; ODD questions go unanswered


### When the Model Fits


- Managers entering new geographies or allocator types benefit most, which is central to any strategy to[win LP capital](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/win-lp-capital-institutional-fundraising) . A U.S.-based manager seeking European institutional exposure, or a well-tenured fund diversifying from family offices into pension capital, can access relationships that would have taken years to build independently.


### When It Doesn't


- First-time funds, sub-scale vehicles, and highly idiosyncratic strategies face a structural mismatch. An allocator who agrees to a cap intro meeting expects institutional readiness: a verifiable track record, a clear capacity story, and back-office infrastructure that holds up under diligence.
- Very niche strategies present a matching problem. The allocator pool that fits a narrow mandate is small, and cap intro networks are not built for precision targeting at that level.


## How the Pre-Meeting Diligence Process Actually Works


The introduction happens fast. What follows it is slower and more deliberate.


Once a prime broker or advisory firm makes the connection, most institutional allocators run an internal screening before they confirm the meeting. That screening has a sequence, and understanding it matters for managers who want to get past the introduction.


### The Intake Step


Many cap intro programs require managers to complete an abbreviated questionnaire before any meeting is scheduled. This is a filter, not the full[fund manager due diligence](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/fund-manager-due-diligence-ir-preparation) review that follows a successful first meeting. The allocator uses it to verify that the manager clears basic thresholds: strategy fit, fund size, track record vintage, and key terms.


Prime brokers also run their own pre-screening. Before a manager enters the cap intro program, the desk assesses whether the manager's profile matches the allocator relationships they can credibly activate. An introduction to the wrong allocator reflects on the prime broker, so the internal bar exists before the external one.


### The Sequence


1. Manager is accepted into the cap intro program after prime broker screening.
2. Allocator receives the manager's profile and abbreviated materials.
3. Allocator may request a pre-meeting DDQ or intake questionnaire.
4. Internal investment or diligence team reviews responses.
5. Meeting is confirmed, deferred, or declined based on that review.


The DDQ at step three is where most managers underestimate the stakes. By the time they complete it, the allocator has already formed an initial impression from the profile materials. The questionnaire either reinforces that impression or contradicts it.


## What the Cap Intro DDQ Typically Covers


Pre-meeting screening questionnaires vary in length, but the question categories are largely consistent across allocator types. Both the[ILPA DDQ](https://ilpa.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/ILPA_Due_Diligence_Questionnaire_v1.2.pdf) and the[AIMA DDQ](https://www.aima.org/sound-practices/due-diligence-questionnaires.html) have defined the standard buckets institutional reviewers rely on, and cap intro screening questionnaires draw from the same categories in abbreviated form.


- Investment strategy and edge: how the fund generates returns, what the sourcing process looks like, and what makes the approach defensible. Allocators want specificity here, not a pitch deck summary.
- Fund economics: management fee, performance fee, hurdle rate, high-water mark, minimum investment, and fund terms. These are threshold filters. A structure outside the allocator's parameters ends the process before the meeting.
- Track record and performance data: audited returns, attribution, vintage, and benchmark context, often compiled with[institutional fundraising tools](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/institutional-fundraising-tools-ai) today. DPI, IRR, and MOIC where applicable. Unaudited figures or cherry-picked periods get noticed.
- Team and key person risk: who runs the strategy, how long they have been together, what succession looks like, and whether any named principals are departure risks.
- Firm infrastructure: prime broker relationships, fund administrator, auditor, legal counsel, and cybersecurity posture. This category screens for institutional readiness before a formal ODD review begins.
- Regulatory standing: registration status, any disciplinary history, and jurisdiction of operation. Managers with unresolved regulatory issues rarely advance past this stage.
- Capacity: how much AUM the strategy can absorb before returns compress, and where the fund currently sits relative to that ceiling.


## The Question Behind the Question: What Allocators Are Really Assessing


Every question in a cap intro DDQ operates on two levels: the literal one on the page, and the unspoken one beneath it.


An allocator asking about fee structure is not primarily interested in the fee. They want to know whether your incentives as a GP are aligned with theirs as a capital provider. A 2-and-20 structure with no hurdle and a soft high-water mark answers that question before the first meeting starts.


Key person questions test organizational depth: whether the strategy survives a departure, whether succession has been thought through, and whether the firm exists beyond its founding principal. A response that lists names without describing roles, decision rights, or backup capacity answers the literal question and misses the actual one.


Strategy questions carry the most interpretive weight. When an allocator asks how you source deals or generate alpha, they are assessing differentiation and capacity simultaneously. A strategy that cannot be described with specificity reads as underdeveloped or not genuinely proprietary. One that sounds compelling but has no clear capacity ceiling raises a separate concern: that performance at current AUM does not predict performance at the scale the allocator would represent.


The firm infrastructure questions are the least glamorous and the most revealing. Prime broker, fund administrator, auditor: these are threshold signals. An allocator running a formal ODD process will go deep on each later. At the screening stage, the question is simpler: does this manager operate like an institution, or are they still building the foundation? These answers function as a proxy for everything the allocator has not yet had time to assess directly.


## How Response Quality Affects Whether the Meeting Happens


Allocators and cap intro desks are processing more managers than they can realistically meet. The screening submission is how they cut the list. A response that is incomplete, inconsistent, or generic does not produce a follow-up question. It produces a pass.


Incomplete answers, often a symptom of[stale DDQ answers](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/ddq-library-decay-stale-answers) , read as one of two things: the manager does not have the data, or they chose not to share it. Neither interpretation advances the conversation. Allocators who cannot verify basic facts from a written submission see no reason to commit time to a meeting that will require the same verification in person.


Generic responses carry a subtler cost. An allocator with a specific mandate reads an undifferentiated strategy description as confirmation that the manager has not engaged with their framework. The response answered the literal question and signaled that no one reviewed who was actually asking. That signal lands before the meeting, not during it.


Consistency failures are the hardest to recover from, because many managers never know they happened. Sophisticated allocators cross-reference current submissions against prior filings when they exist. A figure that differs between this year's submission and last year's without explanation, similar to the mismatches caught during[waterfall and fund returns reconciliation](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/waterfall-lpa-fund-returns-ddq-reconciliation) , a team description that adds or drops names without acknowledging the change, a strategy framing that has shifted without context: any of these can trigger a quiet filter-out before a human reviewer has engaged with the substance. The manager never receives a rejection. The meeting simply never gets scheduled.


## Consistency Across Prior Filings as a Screening Criterion


Most managers treat the cap intro DDQ as a standalone document. Sophisticated allocators do not.


When a prior DDQ, Form ADV filing, or LP correspondence exists, institutional reviewers cross-reference the current submission against it. AUM figures that shifted without explanation, personnel descriptions that added or dropped names silently, strategy language that reframed the approach between submissions: these are not read as updates. They are read as inconsistencies, and inconsistencies trigger quiet disqualifications.


The mechanism has grown more structured as allocator teams have become more systematic, echoing broader[LP DDQ structure bottlenecks](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/lp-ddq-structure-bottlenecks) across the industry. Some institutional reviewers now run scoring against prior submissions before a human analyst engages with a new one. A manager who answered a team stability question one way in 2023 and differently in 2025, with no acknowledgment of what changed, may never reach the meeting stage. The submission passes through a filter the manager did not know existed.


### Form ADV as a Cross-Reference Source


Form ADV is the most commonly overlooked consistency check. It is public, updated annually, and contains firm-level facts that allocators verify against DDQ responses before any conversation begins. A headcount figure that differs between a DDQ and the most recent ADV filing, without explanation, raises a question the manager is not present to answer.


The practical implication, one reason GPs increasingly rely on[LP due diligence tools](https://www.governgpt.com/blog/top-lp-due-diligence-tools-gps-scaling) as they scale, is that response quality cannot be assessed submission by submission. Every DDQ answer a manager sends is part of a longitudinal record, and allocators with access to that record will use it.


## ODD Questions That Appear Before the First Meeting


ODD questions used to live deep in the diligence process, well after an allocator had already decided a manager was worth pursuing. That boundary has shifted. Pre-meeting intake materials now routinely include questions that would have been reserved for a formal ODD review as recently as 2022.


As[RocketDocs notes](https://rocketdocs.com/resources/blog/operational-due-diligence-guide) in their ODD guide, ODD "asks whether a firm's operations can be trusted with capital, and its findings often decide whether an allocation moves forward." Allocators have started pulling that question forward into screening, before committing time to a first meeting.


The categories appearing at the intake stage typically include:


- Fund administrator: who they are, how long the relationship has been in place, and whether they are independent from the GP
- Valuation process: who prices the portfolio, whether there is independent oversight, and what the policy is for hard-to-value assets
- Custody arrangements: where assets are held and under what structure
- Cybersecurity posture: whether the firm has a documented policy, who owns it, and whether any incidents have occurred
- Business continuity: whether a plan exists and has been tested
- Third-party service providers: auditor, legal counsel, compliance consultant, and prime broker relationships


None of these questions require a formal ODD reviewer to ask. They are threshold signals used to determine whether a manager operates with the infrastructure a serious allocator expects before deploying capital. A manager without clear answers at the screening stage signals that the harder questions later will be harder still.

Consistency is an architecture property, not a prompting trick. ## Final Thoughts on Capital Introduction Diligence and Screening


Most managers focus on getting the meeting. The allocators who matter are focused on what arrives before it. Your screening responses, the consistency of your figures across prior submissions, and the specificity of your strategy answers are all being reviewed before anyone picks up the phone. ## FAQ


### What does a cap intro DDQ actually test, and what question is the allocator really asking?


Every question in a capital introduction DDQ operates on two levels: the literal one on the page and the unspoken one beneath it. An allocator asking about key person risk is not primarily asking who runs the strategy. They are asking whether the firm survives a departure and whether succession has been thought through. A question about fee structure is really asking whether GP and LP incentives are aligned. Answering only the literal question satisfies the form; missing the unspoken one ends the process before the meeting.


### How do allocators use prior DDQ filings and Form ADV as cross-reference sources during capital introduction screening?


Sophisticated allocators cross-reference your current submission against prior filings (including Form ADV, prior DDQ responses, and LP correspondence) before a human reviewer engages with the substance. A figure that shifted between 2023 and 2025 without explanation, a team description that dropped a name silently, or a strategy framing that changed without context reads as an inconsistency, not an update. Some institutional reviewers now run automated scoring against prior submissions, meaning a manager can be filtered out before any human opens the file.


### When does a fund benefit from purpose-built DDQ automation software versus a general-purpose AI tool like Claude or ChatGPT?


Purpose-built DDQ automation becomes necessary once your firm has submitted at least two to three prior RFPs and has a meaningful archive of approved questionnaires and source documents. Below that content threshold, a general-purpose AI tool performs comparably; GovernGPT's own sellers acknowledge this directly, with the practical qualification floor sitting around $2.5 to $3 billion AUM. Above it, the advantage is structural: GovernGPT stores the full history of how you have communicated with each LP, guarantees that current answers are consistent with prior filings, and surfaces that history in minutes. No general-purpose model can replicate that, because it has no access to your longitudinal record.


### What should IR heads and CCOs actually test when vetting DDQ automation vendors during a pre-meeting diligence screening workflow?


Test acceptance rate first: the percentage of AI-generated answers the team can send without editing. A tool that requires heavy revision on a large share of outputs adds review burden, not capacity, regardless of its throughput claims; the higher that revision burden, the more clearly the tool has failed its core purpose. Any vendor that cannot cite its acceptance rate has structurally answered the question about output quality. Alongside that, test whether the system can ingest your existing document archive without manual reformatting and produce a working proof-of-concept within a single day; a vendor that cannot do this in evaluation will not do it under a live DDQ deadline.
